subChunks.title: React.memo — Preventing Unnecessary Re-renders
subChunks.hookHtml: By default, when a parent component re-renders, all its children re-render too — even if their props haven't changed. React.memo is the tool that breaks this chain: a wrapped component only re-renders if its props have actually changed. Understanding when this matters — and when it doesn't — is the difference between targeted optimisation and wasted effort.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Why children re-render by default

React re-renders a component when its parent re-renders or when its state/context changes. This is the default. For most components, re-rendering is fast (milliseconds or less) — React only updates the actual DOM when the virtual DOM diff shows changes.

The cost of unnecessary re-renders only matters when:

  • The component has expensive render logic (complex calculations, large trees)
  • It renders many times per second (animation-heavy UIs, real-time dashboards)
  • There are many instances of it in a list (100+ rows)

React.memo — skip re-render when props are unchanged

import { memo } from 'react';

// Without memo: re-renders every time the parent re-renders
function QuestCard({ quest }) {
  return <div>{quest.title}</div>;
}

// With memo: only re-renders when quest prop changes
const QuestCard = memo(function QuestCard({ quest }) {
  return <div>{quest.title}</div>;
});

React.memo uses shallow comparison of props by default. If the prop is a primitive (string, number, boolean), this works perfectly. If the prop is an object or array, the comparison checks reference equality — a new object each render (even with the same contents) will still trigger a re-render.

The trap: new references from the parent

function Parent() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  // ❌ New object every render — memo is bypassed:
  const config = { theme: 'dark', size: 'lg' };

  // ❌ New function every render — memo is bypassed:
  const handleClick = () => doSomething();

  return <MemoChild config={config} onClick={handleClick} />;
}

// ✅ Fix: stabilise with useMemo and useCallback:
const config = useMemo(() => ({ theme: 'dark', size: 'lg' }), []);
const handleClick = useCallback(() => doSomething(), []);

Vex: "React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback form a triangle. memo wraps the child to prevent re-renders. useMemo stabilises object props. useCallback stabilises function props. You need all three for memo to be effective — otherwise you've added cost with no benefit."

Custom comparison function

const QuestCard = memo(
  function QuestCard({ quest }) { return <div>{quest.title}</div>; },
  (prevProps, nextProps) => prevProps.quest.id === nextProps.quest.id
  // Return true to SKIP re-render; false to re-render
);

When NOT to use React.memo

  • When the component already renders fast
  • When the parent rarely re-renders anyway
  • When you haven't measured a real performance problem
  • When the component receives new props frequently regardless

storyBeats.text: Fifty identical lanterns hang in a row. Every time the wind stirs, a puppeteer checks whether each lantern needs adjustment — even the ones on the sheltered side that haven't moved at all. Vex shakes her head. 'Memoize the sheltered ones. Only check the ones that can actually change.'

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback are a system. Memo says 'don't re-render unless props changed.' useMemo says 'this object is stable.' useCallback says 'this function is stable.' All three work together. Without the other two, memo usually fails silently.

storyBeats.speaker: The trio in practice

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a parent/child pair demonstrating memo:

  • ExpensiveChild — wrapped in React.memo. Logs 'ExpensiveChild rendered' on each render. Receives a value prop (string).
  • Parent — has two state values: value (passed to ExpensiveChild) and counter (not passed). Render two buttons: 'Change Value' and 'Increment Counter'
  • With memo: incrementing the counter should NOT re-render ExpensiveChild (log should not fire)
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a <DataTable rows /> component with 100 rows. Each row is a memoised <TableRow row /> component. The parent has a search input (state) and a separate theme toggle (state). Verify via console.log that rows don't re-render when the theme changes but do re-render when their data changes. Use useCallback for any click handlers passed to rows.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain why React.memo alone is often ineffective without useMemo and useCallback. Walk through the scenario where a parent passes an object prop to a memoised child — why does the child still re-render? What three things need to be in place for memo to prevent re-renders?

options: Wraps a component so it only re-renders when its props change (shallow comparison)
Caches the component's rendered output to avoid calling the function
Prevents the component from ever re-rendering
Makes the component's state persist between unmount and remount
questions.answer: Wraps a component so it only re-renders when its props change (shallow comparison)
questions.explanation: React.memo performs a shallow comparison of old and new props before each render. If all props are the same (by reference for objects/functions, by value for primitives), the component skips re-rendering and returns the cached output.

questions.prompt: A memoised component still re-renders on every parent render. The parent passes `onClick={() => doThing()}`. What is the most likely cause?
options: An arrow function creates a new function reference on every render — memo sees a new prop and re-renders
React.memo doesn't work with function props
The onClick is a primitive, not an object, so memo always treats it as changed
React.memo only works on class components
questions.answer: An arrow function creates a new function reference on every render — memo sees a new prop and re-renders
questions.explanation: () => doThing() creates a new function object each render. Shallow comparison sees a different reference and triggers a re-render. Fix: wrap the handler in useCallback so the reference is stable: const handleClick = useCallback(() => doThing(), []).

questions.prompt: A list renders 20 rows. Each row is a simple `<li>` with a name and a checkbox. Should you wrap the row component in React.memo?
options: Probably not — 20 simple rows re-render in less than a millisecond total; memo adds overhead without measurable benefit
Yes — always memo list items to prevent re-renders
Yes — checkboxes cause frequent state changes so memo is essential
No — React.memo cannot be used inside lists
questions.answer: Probably not — 20 simple rows re-render in less than a millisecond total; memo adds overhead without measurable benefit
questions.explanation: React's reconciler is fast. 20 simple component renders take negligible time. React.memo adds comparison cost on every render. For small, fast-rendering lists, memo's overhead can exceed its savings. Profile at 500+ rows with complex content before optimising.
